claims.text: Structural and chemical stability in NbMoTa-type refractory high-entropy nanoalloys is governed by a non-monotonic temperature dependence of atomic diffusion.
A critical temperature exists at which diffusion heterogeneity optimally promotes controlled local atomic rearrangements.
Controlled local rearrangements at the critical temperature maintain metastable chemical disorder.
Temperatures below the optimum provide insufficient atomic mobility and reduce high-temperature performance.
Temperatures above the optimum cause excessive diffusion, ordering or phase separation, and reduced high-temperature performance.
The initial NbMoTa-type nanoalloys are metastable and chemically disordered.
The distribution of atomic migration barriers modulates local chemical ordering.
Diffusion heterogeneity initially increases with temperature and reaches a peak at a critical temperature.
Above the critical temperature, increased diffusion drives enhanced atomic ordering or phase separation.
Independent surface-segregation controls can establish whether measured diffusion heterogeneity is intrinsic rather than skewed by surface segregation.
A distinct peak in diffusion heterogeneity should occur at an intermediate temperature between 600°C and 1000°C.
Below the diffusion-heterogeneity peak, limited mobility leaves the alloy metastably disordered.
Above the diffusion-heterogeneity peak, microstructural and spectroscopic measurements should reveal ordering or phase separation.
Poorly controlled surface segregation would produce more monotonic or less pronounced diffusion behavior than the proposed controlled experiment.
The proposed behavior is expected to occur within 600°C to 1000°C.
Excessive surface segregation may invalidate the proposed mechanism by altering effective diffusion profiles.
Failure to observe a non-monotonic diffusion-heterogeneity peak at an intermediate temperature would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says lower-temperature insufficient mobility reduces performance because optimal rearrangements are needed to maintain disorder, whereas the predicted outcome says limited mobility itself leaves the alloy metastably disordered. The relationship between preserved disorder and reduced stability/performance is therefore unresolved.

The mechanism expects surface-segregation controls to show that the correlation is intrinsic and not significantly skewed by segregation, but the falsification rule treats a failure of segregation control to alter that correlation as falsifying. An unchanged correlation after control would ordinarily be consistent with the stated intrinsic mechanism.
